newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FEATURE-Rio battles to decontaminate Guanabara Bay.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Rio battles to decontaminate Guanabara Bay.

text.p: The beauty of Rio de Janeiro's Guanabara Bay as it curves around world-famous Sugar Loaf mountain and the city's coastline has been immortalised on millions of postcards.

But most locals would not swim in its waters despite the city's stifling heat. For many years now the fish have been dying, the mangroves have been wilting and white vultures circle where seagulls used to fly. The stench that drifts across the murky waters in parts of the bay and the dead fish and garbage floating on the oil-patched surface were one reason Rio never even came close to succeeding in its bid to stage the 2004 Olympic Games.

As hosts of the 1992 Earth Summit, Rio's authorities promised to clean up the bay, launching in 1994 what they described as Latin America's biggest environmental clean-up programme. But the $867 million effort financed by Rio state, the Interamerican Development Bank (IADB) and Japan's Overseas Economic Cooperation Fund (OECF) has been marred by delays, controversy and accusations of political opportunism.

Environmentalists say the project, which is using almost 90 percent of its funds to improve sanitation, has the wrong priorities. "This programme is being sold as an environmental clean-up programme when it's actually a sanitation programme," said Sergio Ricardo, a consultant to the state legislature's environmental commission.

"The programme does not address all the environmental problems of the bay," he said. "Not one penny is being spent to regenerate fishing, to save the mangroves or to stop the silting up of the bay, which is the most serious problem."
ENOUGH SEWAGE TO FILL A SOCCER STADIUM

The roughly eight million people living around Guanabara throw hundreds of tonnes of garbage into the bay every day and enough raw sewage to fill Rio's world famous Maracana soccer stadium. An oil refinery, two commercial ports and some 6,000 industrial firms add their share of waste such as oil and heavy metals to the lethal cocktail.

The pollution of Guanabara Bay goes back a long way, to the arrival of the Portuguese in Brazil 400 years ago. Ever since, the 188-square-mile (300-sq km) bay has been used as a garbage dump, with pollution reaching unsustainable levels in the last 10 to 15 years.

Twenty years ago as many as 20,000 fishermen made a living fishing the waters of the bay, but today the numbers have dwindled to less than 3,000. "Eighteen years ago you could fish in the bay; now you have to sail out of the bay to get fish," Domingos Ferreira Alves said, looking out over the bay from the garbage-littered shores of the Tabiacanga fishing village where he has lived for 30 years.

The tragedy of Guanabara Bay is just another example of Latin American environmental ruin, which has continued at an alarming rate in recent years because governments often do not have the money or the political will to stop the destruction.

"Serious environmental policies are completely lacking in this country and in this state," said geologist and geographer Elmo Silva Amador, who has been studying Guanabara's pollution since the 1970s. "The clean-up will almost make no difference. People living around the bay will see some improvements but the bay itself won't benefit much."
OFFICIAL IS CONFIDENT OF CUTTING POLLUTION

But the vice-governor of Rio de Janeiro state, Luiz Paulo Correa da Rocha, who is in charge of the project, is confident pollution levels will be cut significantly by 1999, when work agreed to under the financing scheme must be completed. He said the work was proceeding at such a rate that authorities had almost made up for a one-year delay at the start of the programme caused by legal and managerial wrangling, which cost the state government $1.2 million in fines by the IADB.
"The programme is moving full-steam ahead. Our aim to reduce pollution by 50 percent will be achieved by 1999," he said.

The programme foresees six new garbage disposal plants, 7 new sewage treatment plants and 10 new water reservoirs among other things. Rocha said the bay would also benefit from related projects including another $130 million spent on water treatment plants and $300 million being spent to regenerate shantytowns around the bay.

But environmentalists doubt pollution levels will be cut by more than 30 percent at most and accuse state officials of operating the programme for political gains, often neglecting what is best for the bay. They argue the state is losing out on additional funds and know-how by not collaborating with the 13 municipalities located around the bay and by not consulting with all those who have an interest in the clean-up.
"The state doesn't want to involve the mayors because Rio's state governor wants all the praise for cleaning up the bay," Ricardo said. "This is the perverse situation of Brazilian politics."
